title.en: 4.1 Symbols on a production drawing: machining, geometric, welding, piping
title.gu: 4.1 Symbols on a production drawing: machining, geometric, welding, piping

body.en:
What the symbol orders

A machined surface is never perfectly smooth; its required finish is specified by the surface-texture symbol placed on the surface line (or on a Leader/witness line from it), read from the same direction as the dimensions. The check-mark like symbol has three standard forms: the basic symbol (two unequal strokes) used when only 'a finished surface' is meant; with a bar across the top = material removal by machining is required; with a circle in the V = material removal is prohibited (surface left as cast/forged, e.g. 'do not machine - sealing face as cast').

The value: roughness Ra

Above the symbol's arm sits the roughness value, normally Ra in micrometres (arithmetical average roughness): Ra 12.5 rough turning/casting finish, Ra 6.3 general turning, Ra 3.2 good turning/reaming, Ra 1.6 fine turning/broaching, Ra 0.8 grinding, Ra 0.4/0.2 lapping/honing. Equivalent roughness grades N1-N12 (N8 = Ra 3.2, N7 = 1.6, N6 = 0.8...). Additional entries can state the manufacturing process ('ground'), machining allowance, sampling length and lay direction (the direction of the surface pattern: = parallel, perpendicular, X crossed, M multi-directional, C circular, R radial).

Why it is on the drawing at all

Finish controls function (bearing journals, sealing faces, fatigue strength, friction and wear) and cost: specifying grinding where turning suffices wastes money; the reverse scraps the part. Every surface of a production drawing carries either its own symbol or is covered by the general note in the title block ('all surfaces Ra 6.3 unless otherwise stated').

h.en: 4.1 Geometric symbols (GD&T) and the feature control frame
h.gu: 4.1 Geometric symbols (GD&T) and the feature control frame

body.en:
Why size tolerance alone is not enough

A shaft can satisfy its diameter limits yet be bent, oval or tapered - size within tolerance, geometry wrong, assembly failed. GD&T (Geometric Dimensioning and Tolerancing, ISO 1101 / ASME Y14.5 practice taught with BIS conventions) controls the form, orientation, location and runout of features with a stated tolerance zone, measured from datums (the reference planes/axes of the part).

The 14 characteristic symbols (diagram md4_gdt)

  • Form (no datum): straightness, flatness, circularity (roundness), cylindricity.
  • Orientation (datum needed): parallelism, perpendicularity, angularity.
  • Location (datum needed): position, concentricity/coaxiality, symmetry.
  • Runout: circular runout, total runout. Plus profile of a line/surface.

Feature control frame - the sentence of GD&T

The rectangular frame reads left to right: [geometric characteristic symbol] [tolerance value - prefixed by dia. symbol when the zone is cylindrical] [datum letter(s), in order of precedence]. A datum is declared by a datum-feature symbol (capital letter in a box on a triangle touching the feature). Example: position dia. 0.05 relative to datums A and B (drawn in the diagram) means the axis of the hole must lie inside a 0.05 mm diameter cylindrical zone whose axis is at the theoretically exact position fixed from A and B. Unit 3 gave the size system; GD&T is its geometric completion - both appear together on every modern production drawing (Practical 4).

h.en: 4.1 Weld-joint symbols as per BIS 813 and supplementary symbols
h.gu: 4.1 Weld-joint symbols as per BIS 813 and supplementary symbols

body.en:
The reference-line system

A weld is specified by a symbol placed on a horizontal reference line with an arrow touching the joint: the symbol drawn below the line describes the weld on the arrow side of the joint; above the line, the other side. Size is written to the left of the symbol, length to the right (stitch/pitch as length x pitch). A circle at the arrow junction = weld all around; a small flag = field (site) weld; a tail at the end carries the welding process/specification reference. (BIS 813 follows the ISO 2553 system.)

Basic symbols to sketch (diagram)

Fillet (triangle), square butt (two parallel strokes), single-V butt, single-bevel, plug/slot (rectangle), spot (circle), seam (circle with cross line), edge weld; U/J variants add a curved stroke. Supplementary symbols modify the contour: straight/flush, convex, concave finish lines above the symbol, and the 'weld all around' circle and field flag.

Fluid and pipe-fitting symbols (same card family)

P&ID and piping drawings use their own symbol set: gate/globe/check/non-return valves (bow-tie variants), elbows, tee, reducer (concentric/eccentric trapezoids), flange pair (double line), pump (circle with triangle), strainer, steam trap, pipe crossing vs junction (dot = joined, gap = not joined). Reading them fluently is part of this syllabus item; they are drawn single-line and labelled by line number, not to scale.

title.en: 4.1-4.2 Fasteners, and the production drawing of an assembly
title.gu: 4.1-4.2 Fasteners, and the production drawing of an assembly

h.en: 4.1 Sketches of threads, studs, screws, nuts, bolts, rivets and keys
h.gu: 4.1 Sketches of threads, studs, screws, nuts, bolts, rivets and keys

body.en:
Threads

ISO metric threads dominate (designation M12 x 1.5: nominal dia. 12 mm, pitch 1.5 mm; coarse pitch is implied when pitch is omitted). Threads are never drawn as true helixes in production drawings: conventional representation - external thread: major diameter thick line, minor diameter thin line, thread run-out at the end; internal thread the reverse (minor thick in section). Chamfer at the thread start equals roughly the minor diameter circle. Profile families to recognise: ISO metric (60 deg V), square, ACME (29 deg), buttress, knuckle - chosen by load and motion duty.

The standard fasteners (sketch each from the diagram)

  • Bolt and nut: hexagonal head/nut across-flats = approx. 1.5 x nominal dia. plus clearance conventions (hex width across corners approx. 2d legacy rule used in exercises is 1.5d AF), washer under the nut; bolted joint drawn with the nut on the far plate, thread length approx. 2d + 6 mm grip rule in exercises.
  • Stud: threaded at both ends with a plain middle; the screwed end length approx. 1d-1.5d into the body (depends on body material); used where a through bolt is impossible and frequent removal happens at the nut end only (cylinder heads).
  • Screws: set screws (grub, with point types) lock pulleys/keys; machine screws (cheese/pan/CSK heads) with screwdriver/Allen drives.
  • Rivets: permanent joints for sheet/plate (boilers, structures, aircraft): snap (button), pan, countersunk (flush), flat heads; rivet dia. by Unwin's rule d = 6 x sqrt(t) mm for plate thickness t.
  • Keys: transmit torque between shaft and hub: rectangular sunk (parallel), woodruff (segmental, self-aligning for tapered shafts), feather (sliding), gib-head (withdrawable). Key size follows shaft diameter tables.

In sectional assembly views

Bolts, nuts, studs, screws, keys and shafts are conventionally shown unsectioned (Unit 2 rule) - learn to recognise them whole inside hatched housings.

h.en: 4.2 Production drawing of a simple assembly (5-6 components) including GD&T
h.gu: 4.2 Production drawing of a simple assembly (5-6 components) including GD&T

body.en:
What a production drawing package contains

For a simple assembly (e.g. a bench vice, plummer block, flange coupling, tool post - 5-6 manufactured components each involving turning, drilling, milling, grinding operations) the production set is:

  • Detail (part) drawings - one per component: complete views (with sections), all dimensions with limits/fits, surface-texture symbols on functional faces, GD&T frames where geometry matters (perpendicular bore, positional bolt holes), material and heat-treatment notes, title block.
  • Assembly drawing - the parts assembled, normally in section, with balloon numbers keyed to the parts list; only assembly-relevant dimensions (overall, centre distances, fits written as 50 H7/g6 between mating parts).
  • Parts list / BOM - part number, name, material, quantity, standard-part specification (Unit 5, Card 5.2).

Working sequence (the Practical 4 routine)

1) Decide datums and fits at the interfaces first (which surfaces locate, slide, or fix - from Units 3). 2) Detail each part so mating surfaces carry matching dimensions from common datums (avoid tolerance pile-up). 3) Put GD&T only where function demands (positional tolerance on hole patterns, perpendicularity of faces that seat). 4) Assign finishes by duty (sliding face finer than a free face). 5) Assemble mentally on paper: check every dimension chain closes and every part can be manufactured and assembled in a real sequence. A production drawing is finished when a stranger can make and assemble the product from it without asking a single question - the standard these notes hold every card to.

h.en: Practical 4: Draw production drawing with GD&T and drafting symbols
h.gu: Practical 4: Draw production drawing with GD&T and drafting symbols

body.en:
Objective (Syllabus Practical 4)

Prepare the production drawing of a simple mechanical assembly (5-6 components) applying limits/fits, GD&T and drafting symbols - sketchbook first, then A2 sheet.

Procedure

  • Step 1: Select/obtain the assembly (bench vice, flange coupling, plummer block...); list components, their functions and interfaces.
  • Step 2: Fix fits at each interface (clearance for sliding, transition for location, interference for permanent) in H7-based designations.
  • Step 3: Draw detail views of each component with dimensions, limit designations, surface-texture symbols and at least two GD&T feature control frames (e.g. position of holes, perpendicularity of a seating face).
  • Step 4: Draw the sectional assembly view with balloons and parts list; add weld symbols if any joint is welded.
  • Step 5: Self-check: every mating pair shares a common datum dimension; no surface lacks a finish requirement; title blocks complete.

Result (report format)

Submit the sheet set (details + assembly). Conclusion: table of the fits chosen with reasons, and the GD&T controls applied with the function each protects.

h.en: Q1. Draw the surface-texture (machining) symbol. How are 'machining required' and 'machining prohibited' shown? What does Ra 3.2 mean?
h.gu: Q1. Draw the surface-texture (machining) symbol. How are 'machining required' and 'machining prohibited' shown? What does Ra 3.2 mean?

body.en:
Model answer

The symbol is a check-mark of two unequal strokes placed on the surface. A horizontal bar closing the top of the symbol means material removal by machining is required; a circle drawn in the V means material removal is prohibited (surface to remain as cast/forged). The roughness value is written above the arm: Ra 3.2 means the arithmetical mean roughness of the surface must not exceed 3.2 micrometres - a good turned/reamed finish (grade N8). The symbol is applied on the surface line or a Leader and read from the dimension side.

h.en: Q2. Explain the structure of a GD&T feature control frame with an example.
h.gu: Q2. Explain the structure of a GD&T feature control frame with an example.

body.en:
Model answer

The feature control frame is a rectangle divided into compartments read left to right: first the geometric characteristic symbol (e.g. position), second the tolerance value - prefixed with the diameter symbol when the tolerance zone is cylindrical - and then the datum reference letters in their order of precedence. Example: [position | dia. 0.05 | A | B] applied to a hole means: the axis of the actual hole must lie within a cylindrical tolerance zone 0.05 mm in diameter, located at the theoretically exact position established from datum A (primary) and datum B (secondary). The frame is attached to the feature by a Leader or extension line, and datums themselves are declared with datum-feature symbols (letter in a box on a triangle).

h.en: Q4. Explain the weld symbol system of BIS 813: reference line, arrow side and other side, size and length positions.
h.gu: Q4. Explain the weld symbol system of BIS 813: reference line, arrow side and other side, size and length positions.

body.en:
Model answer

The weld is called out on a horizontal reference line whose arrow touches the joint. The basic weld symbol placed below the reference line specifies the weld on the arrow side; placed above, it specifies the other side. The weld size (e.g. fillet leg 6 mm) is written to the left of the symbol and its length to the right (intermittent welds as length x pitch). A circle at the junction of arrow and reference line orders welding all around the joint; a flag at the junction denotes a field/site weld; the tail at the far end quotes the process or specification. Sketch: 6 written left of a fillet triangle below the line means a 6 mm fillet on the arrow side (diagram md4_weld).

h.en: Q5. Differentiate between a bolt and a stud. Where is a stud used?
h.gu: Q5. Differentiate between a bolt and a stud. Where is a stud used?

body.en:
Model answer

A bolt has a head at one end and an external thread at the other; it passes through clearance holes in both parts and is tightened with a nut. A stud has no head; it is threaded at both ends with a plain portion between - one end is screwed permanently into a tapped hole in one component and the other parts are clamped by a nut on the free end. Studs are used where a through bolt cannot be inserted or where the joint is opened frequently at one side only - cylinder heads, gear-box covers, turbine casings - because the tapped hole in the main body is not worn by repeated screwing.

h.en: Q6. Name four types of keys and state one use of each.
h.gu: Q6. Name four types of keys and state one use of each.

body.en:
Model answer

(1) Rectangular sunk (parallel) key - general torque transmission between shaft and hub, e.g. pulley on a line shaft. (2) Woodruff key - segmental key seating itself in a semicircular pocket; for light drives and tapered shaft ends (machine-tool arbors). (3) Feather key - fixed to one member and sliding in the other; for hubs that must slide axially while rotating, e.g. gearbox sliding gears. (4) Gib-head key - sunk key with a raised head so it can be drifted out for removal; used on large pulleys where the hub must be removable.

h.en: Q7. How are external and internal threads represented conventionally in a drawing?
h.gu: Q7. How are external and internal threads represented conventionally in a drawing?

body.en:
Model answer

Threads are not drawn as true helixes. For an external thread, the major (crest) diameter is drawn with a thick continuous line and the minor (root) diameter with a thin continuous line; in the end view the minor diameter is a thin circle of about three-quarter circumference. For an internal thread the convention is reversed in section: the minor diameter is thick and the major diameter thin. The usable thread length is bounded by a thick line; the run-out/chamfer is shown at the start. Designation is by note, e.g. M20 (ISO metric, 20 mm nominal, coarse pitch).

h.en: Q8. What items must a production drawing of an assembly contain?

q.en: Bolt vs stud - one line.
q.gu: Bolt vs stud - one line.

a.en: A bolt has a head and needs a nut through clear holes; a stud is headless, threaded both ends, one end fixed in a tapped hole - for joints opened repeatedly from one side only (cylinder heads).

a.gu: Conventionally: external thread - major diameter thick line, minor diameter thin line (thin 3/4 circle in end view); internal - reversed in section. Never as a true helix; labelled 'M20'.

title.en: Practical 4: Draw production drawing with GD&T and drafting symbols
title.gu: Practical 4: Draw production drawing with GD&T and drafting symbols

body.en:
Objective (Syllabus Practical 4)

Prepare the production drawing of a simple mechanical assembly (5-6 components) applying limits/fits, GD&T and drafting symbols - sketchbook first, then A2 sheet.

Procedure

  • Step 1: Select/obtain the assembly (bench vice, flange coupling, plummer block...); list components, their functions and interfaces.
  • Step 2: Fix fits at each interface (clearance for sliding, transition for location, interference for permanent) in H7-based designations.
  • Step 3: Draw detail views of each component with dimensions, limit designations, surface-texture symbols and at least two GD&T feature control frames (e.g. position of holes, perpendicularity of a seating face).
  • Step 4: Draw the sectional assembly view with balloons and parts list; add weld symbols if any joint is welded.
  • Step 5: Self-check: every mating pair shares a common datum dimension; no surface lacks a finish requirement; title blocks complete.

Result (report format)

Submit the sheet set (details + assembly). Conclusion: table of the fits chosen with reasons, and the GD&T controls applied with the function each protects.
